item.title: Amazon Polly Generative Engine Upgrade Adds New Voices and Low‑Latency Streaming
item.description:
Amazon Polly Generative Engine Upgrade Adds New Voices and Low‑Latency Streaming

Amazon Polly’s Generative engine has been upgraded and is now generally available, bringing more natural, expressive speech and low‑latency streaming.

🔍 Overview

  • The upgrade delivers more expressive, more accurate speech output with low latency.
  • It is a drop‑in upgrade for existing generative voices; voice names and API calls remain unchanged.

⚙️ Key Details

  • More natural and accurate speech output.
  • Low‑latency streaming for real‑time applications.
  • 14 new voices across 9 locales.
  • Hindi and Finnish generative voices are now generally available for the first time.
  • No changes to code, voice names, or API calls are required.
  • Same pay‑as‑you‑go pricing; no cost increase or new SKU.
  • Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML) support for fine‑grained control.
  • Fully managed AWS service reliability.

🚀 Availability

  • Generally available in production.
  • Existing applications continue to work unchanged.
  • New applications use the same SynthesizeSpeech API to access the larger voice catalog.

🧩 How it Works

  • Uses a standard Amazon Polly API call to build speech applications.
  • The Bi‑Di Streaming API StartSpeechSynthesisStream streams text and receives audio simultaneously.
  • Voices can reflect emotion and prosody based on text input without manual setup.
  • Well‑suited for real‑time use cases like voice agents and bespoke characters in games.

💡 Why it Matters

  • Improved voice quality and accuracy at the same price.
  • Supports contact centers, LLM‑based agentic applications, media, e‑learning, accessibility, and other production use cases.
  • Allows caching and replay of static prompts with no additional cost.
  • Combines quality, performance, and cost efficiency for a wide range of production workloads.
Locale Availability
Hindi General Availability
Finnish General Availability

#AmazonPolly #TextToSpeech #AWS #GenerativeAI

Source: Amazon Polly delivers a major upgrade to its Generative engine | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Streaming Text-to-Speech with Kokoro-82M Reduces Voice Agent Latency
item.description:
Streaming Text-to-Speech with Kokoro-82M Reduces Voice Agent Latency

A customer asks an AI voice agent a question and waits. The agent already has an answer and is midway through generating a long, multi‑paragraph response, but the customer hears nothing for five seconds. By the time an answer arrives, the customer is frustrated, confused, and no longer paying attention. Text‑to‑speech integrations create exactly that gap: a one‑sentence response might generate in 600 ms, but the full response takes five seconds, and the integration waits for all of it before synthesis starts.

🔍 Overview

  • Problem: Silent gap between language generation and audio playback causes user frustration.
  • Solution: Stream each sentence to a hosted Kokoro‑82M text‑to‑speech (TTS) model on Amazon SageMaker AI as soon as the agent produces it, so synthesis begins on sentence one instead of after the full response.
  • The approach also covers the transport needed to get audio back to a browser and the practical cost considerations.

🧩 How it works

  1. The AI agent generates text sentence by sentence.
  2. Each sentence is sent immediately to a SageMaker real‑time endpoint hosting the Kokoro‑82M model.
  3. The TTS model synthesizes the audio for that sentence while the agent continues generating subsequent sentences.
  4. Audio streams to the client browser as soon as it is ready, eliminating the initial silent gap.

⚙️ Key details

  • Model: Kokoro‑82M has 82 million parameters, small enough to run cheaply on a single mid‑tier GPU instance.
  • Endpoint: Runs in a custom container on a SageMaker AI real‑time endpoint (ml.g5.xlarge GPU instance).
  • Container routes:
    Route Description
    POST /invocations Streams a response for one complete input
    WS /invocations-bidirectional-stream Keeps one connection open across many messages in both directions
  • Bidirectional transport uses binary WebSocket frames; a typical Starlette receive_text() handler fails because the message lacks a text key, raising KeyError('text'). A generic exception handler that forwards str(e) masks the framing issue as a missing field error.
  • Infrastructure requirements:
    • AWS account with permissions to create SageMaker AI endpoints and invoke Bedrock models.
    • IAM actions: sagemaker:CreateEndpoint, sagemaker:CreateEndpointConfig, sagemaker:CreateModel, sagemaker:InvokeEndpointWithBidirectionalStream, bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream.
    • Amazon ECR repository for the container image.
    • AWS CDK v2 (installed and bootstrapped), Python 3.12+, uv, Docker, and Boto3 supporting invoke_endpoint_with_bidirectional_stream.
    • The sample container pins an older PyTorch version with advisory PYSEC‑2026‑2286; review and upgrade before any non‑proof‑of‑value use.

🚀 Deployment steps

  1. speech‑infra deploy – provisions the Kokoro‑82M endpoint:
    • Creates foundation and model‑cache stacks that set up IAM roles and sync model weights to Amazon S3.
    • Builds the container image, creates the SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and the endpoint.
  2. agent‑infra deploy – provisions the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime that hosts the Strands agent and calls the newly created endpoint (deploy the endpoint first).
  3. Ensure the SageMaker AI real‑time endpoint’s Docker image declares com.amazonaws.sagemaker.capabilities.bidirectional-streaming=true.
  4. Use the provided CLI tools (wrapping AWS CDK stacks) to apply the infrastructure.

💡 Why it matters

  • Latency: Audio playback can start after the first sentence is generated (≈600 ms) instead of waiting for the full response (≈5 s).
  • Cost: Kokoro‑82M runs on a single ml.g5.xlarge GPU, keeping inference cost low for a voice agent handling real traffic.
  • User experience: Removes the silent gap, keeping customers engaged and attentive.
  • Reusable transport: The blog also explains both HTTP and bidirectional WebSocket transports and their practical cost in a browser setting.

#AI #TextToSpeech #SageMaker #Streaming

Source: Stream low-latency speech from AI agents using Kokoro TTS on Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Study Releases Open-Source Text-to-Speech Voices for Kurdish
item.description:
Study Releases Open-Source Text-to-Speech Voices for Kurdish

A recent study has released three Kurdish voices, 35 hours of recorded speech, and a descriptive paper, all available for free download to address the lack of technology capable of reading Kurdish aloud.

🚀 Availability

  • Three Kurdish voices
  • 35 hours of recorded speech
  • A paper describing the work

⚙️ Key details

  • Data Source: The voices were built from three people reading prepared texts.
  • Performance: While the voices sound fluent, they represent the reading styles of the speakers rather than Kurdish as a whole.
  • Technical Issues:
    • A coding fault mishandles long numbers.
    • Test recordings are left unlabeled among training data.
    • A settings file lists equipment that was never used.

💡 Why it matters

  • Kurdish is spoken by millions, but has limited technology for reading text aloud.
  • The use of prepared texts removes much everyday and regional speech, and does not account for major regional and written variations in Kurdish.
  • Compared to English and German, Kurdish has far less linguistic description and dictionary support to help identify wrong pronunciations, meaning software choices can go unchecked.
  • There is a discrepancy between reports, as the download page claims a stronger result than the paper reports and recommends one voice for general use.

#Kurdish #TextToSpeech #OpenSource #AI

Source: Assessing the Reusability of Public Speech Resources for Low-Resource Languages: A Central Kurdish Case Study

item.title: 🎭 PlayDiffusion: Fixing the Broken Words in AI Speech
item.description:
🎭 PlayDiffusion: Fixing the Broken Words in AI Speech

Summary: Discover how Play.AI’s innovative diffusion model solves one of the most frustrating limitations in AI speech synthesis—the inability to edit specific words without compromising audio quality. This breakthrough approach maintains prosody and speaker characteristics across edits, enabling seamless audio modifications that were previously impossible with traditional autoregressive models.

🔊 The Speech Editing Problem

Imagine you’ve just generated a beautifully synthesized voice clip saying “The answer is out there, Neo. Go grab it!” But then you realize—you need the name to be “Trinity” instead. With traditional text-to-speech systems, you’re stuck with unpleasant choices:

🔄 Regenerate the entire sentence (risking different prosody throughout) ✂️ Replace just “Neo” (creating obvious audio discontinuities) ↩️ Regenerate from the edit point (potentially changing the rhythm of what follows)

This frustrating limitation stems from the fundamentally linear way conventional autoregressive transformer models work—they generate audio left-to-right, making isolated edits nearly impossible without compromising naturalness and coherence.

As developers or content creators, this is more than a minor inconvenience. It’s a significant workflow barrier that forces us to accept imperfect audio or spend excessive time regenerating and fine-tuning output.

🧠 Enter PlayDiffusion: Non-Autoregressive Speech Magic

Play.AI has tackled this problem head-on with PlayDiffusion, leveraging a 𝗻𝗼𝗻-𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗴𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 that makes precise audio edits possible while preserving surrounding context.

Here’s how the PlayDiffusion process works:

  1. 🎵 Tokenization - The audio waveform gets encoded into discrete tokens, creating a compact representation of the speech

  2. 🎭 Masking - Only the portion that needs editing (like the word “Neo”) gets masked out

  3. ✨ Diffusion-Based Denoising - A specialized diffusion model, conditioned on the revised text, denoises just the masked region

  4. 🔄 Decoding - The resulting token sequence gets transformed back into speech using a BigVGAN decoder model, maintaining the original speaker’s voice characteristics

This approach differs fundamentally from traditional models by allowing the algorithm to simultaneously consider both past and future context when generating the edited segment—something that’s impossible with the one-directional nature of autoregressive models.

🛠️ Technical Innovations Behind the Magic

What makes PlayDiffusion particularly clever is the architecture modifications necessary to achieve this capability:

𝗡𝗼𝗻-𝗖𝗮𝘂𝘀𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

Unlike standard decoder-only language models (think GPT), which can only see “backward” in a sequence, PlayDiffusion implements 𝘯𝘰𝘯-𝘤𝘢𝘶𝘴𝘢𝘭 𝘢𝘵𝘵𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘩𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘴. This architectural choice allows tokens to attend to past, present, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 future tokens—critical for maintaining coherent transitions when editing mid-sequence.

🗣️ 𝗦𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗿 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗱𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴

The model incorporates speaker embeddings derived from a pre-trained model that maps waveforms to fixed-size vectors. This ensures the edited segments maintain the original voice’s unique characteristics—tone, timbre, accent and all.

📊 𝗢𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗲𝗱 𝗧𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

To boost computational efficiency, PlayDiffusion uses a custom BPE (Byte Pair Encoding) tokenizer with only 10,000 text tokens. This significantly reduces embedding table size while maintaining high audio quality.

🔍 Inside the Training Process

The training approach is particularly fascinating, built on a masking strategy similar to MaskGCT [3]. During training:

  1. Random percentages of audio tokens get masked
  2. The model learns to predict these masked tokens using:
    • Surrounding unmasked audio context
    • Text input
    • Speaker embedding information

This is formalized in their training loss function:

L𝘮𝘢𝘴𝘬 = −∑(m𝘵,𝘪 ⋅ log pθ(x𝘪|X𝘵,C))

Where m𝘵,𝘪 equals 1 for masked tokens and 0 otherwise, essentially focusing the learning exclusively on predicting the masked portions.

🚀 Iterative Inference for Quality Results

The inference process is equally clever, using an iterative approach:

  1. 🎯 Start with a fully masked token sequence
  2. 🧩 Generate initial predictions for all tokens
  3. 📊 Assign confidence scores based on prediction probabilities
  4. 🔄 Adaptively remask tokens with the lowest confidence
  5. 🔁 Repeat the process, gradually decreasing the number of masked tokens

This iterative refinement ensures the model focuses its efforts on areas of highest uncertainty first, gradually building a coherent, natural-sounding edit that blends seamlessly with the surrounding audio.

💭 Why This Matters

PlayDiffusion represents a significant leap forward in speech synthesis technology. Previously, the rigid nature of autoregressive models meant that any change, no matter how small, often required regenerating entire audio segments—wasting computation resources and creating workflow bottlenecks.

With this approach, we’re seeing the beginnings of truly 𝗲𝗱𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘀𝘆𝗻𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗲𝗰𝗵, where modifications can be made with the same granularity and ease as text editing. The implications extend beyond simple word replacements—this technology enables:

  • 🎬 More efficient voiceover workflows with rapid iteration
  • 🌐 Localization projects that can selectively modify proper nouns
  • 🎮 Dynamic game content with consistent voice character
  • 📱 More responsive voice assistants and audio interfaces

The next time you need to change “Neo” to “Trinity” in your synthesized audio, you won’t need to regenerate everything—just the part that needs changing, seamlessly integrated with the surrounding context. Isn’t that the future of speech synthesis we’ve all been waiting for?
